newsitem.title: GERMANY: ADIDAS CEO SEES STRONG SALES GROWTH TO CONTINUE.
newsitem.headline: ADIDAS CEO SEES STRONG SALES GROWTH TO CONTINUE.

text.p: Adidas AG chief executive Robert Louis-Dreyfus said on Tuesday that he expected sales at the German sports brand to remain strong and keep up the recent blistering pace.
"The trend at 30 percent top-line growth will continue for the rest of the year," Louis-Dreyfus told Reuters in a telephone interview. "In general, we are very encouraged."
Louis-Dreyfus said sales during the fourth quarter, traditionally a weak period for sportswear manufacturers, would be up or down about two to three percent from previous quarterly growth rates.
Adidas earlier on Tuesday said third quarter sales rose 35 percent to 1.47 billion marks, while net income rose 17 percent to 140 million marks.
He said sales had been strong in Britain, Sweden and Spain with sales growth rates above 30 percent but that France, Switzerland and Austria had not performed as expected.

Louis-Dreyfus said adidas was gearing up for the rollout of clothing ahead of the Christmas season tied to its recent sponsorship deal for the 1998 soccer World Cup, an event he said would confirm adidas as a top global sportwear name.
He said the Herzogenaurach-based brand, well known for its three-stripe logo, was seeking to at least break even from its costs against sales of event-related items.
"We may not break even but we won't be far away," he said, declining to predict how much adidas would spend on the event.

"My perception is that we are the No. 1 in soccer and if you are the top in soccer you need to have the single clubs but also you have to be the main sponsor of the most important event, which is the World Cup," he said.
Some industry analysts have warned that adidas' financial performance could be hampered by costs related to the event but Louis-Dreyfus downplayed the impact.
"It's an investment. But frankly it is an investment we pay over two years, so that whatever the number we do not have it in one year, as we did with the Olympics," he said.

He declined to quantify what goodwill benefits adidas expected to see in its overall product sales due to the event sponsorship, which is the first time a sportswear maker has bought the global licensing rights to the World Cup.
"That's the cherry on the cake," he said. "We have hopes and we will see what happens."
Louis-Dreyfus said adidas has shifted its marketing strategy to launch the sale of related items well ahead of the event instead of waiting until a few months ahead of time.
"There has been a change in strategy to put products out earlier," he said.
Adidas pinned some of its third-quarter performance on above-average sales growth in the U.S., where sales rose 44 percent to $314 million from $218 million in the 1995 period.
Adidas, which is now the No. 3 sports shoe maker in the U.S. behind Nike and Reebok , saw particularly strong growth in the sale of running shoes.

"Our running footwear has been booming," he said, noting the company would sell about two million pairs of running shoes in the U.S. in 1996. "Next year in America, at least from the backlog order, it could be up 100 percent in running."
